title: AI Takeoff Speed & Loss of Control
scope: Takeoff speed and loss of human control. Transition dynamics, not timelines or the risk case.

overview.summary: Whether advanced AI arrives as a sharp jump or gradually, and whether control is lost in one moment, by slow drift — or not at all.
overview.scope_covered: The transition to superhuman AI: takeoff speed, recursive self-improvement, decisive takeover vs slow disempowerment, warning shots, and what each bet implies for safety strategy.
overview.scope_excluded: Near-term harms (bias, jobs, deepfakes), machine consciousness, alignment technique details, and the specific machinery of AI governance regimes.
overview.why_now: Frontier labs now publicly target fully automated AI research within a few years, turning the takeoff-speed bet from thought experiment into a near-term planning assumption; in one year of resurveying, AI researchers’ median date for human-level systems moved thirteen years closer.

stats.label: AI task-length doubling time · autonomous benchmark tasks
stats.note: The length of tasks AI agents can complete on their own, at 50% reliability, has doubled roughly every 7 months for the last 6 years.
stats.detail: METR, an independent AI evaluations group, measured this by testing models on software and research tasks of increasing length, from seconds-long tasks in 2019 to roughly hour-long tasks by 2025. Extrapolating implies week-long autonomous tasks within a few years, but METR itself flags that the trend could bend if it depends on a specific capability mix that stops scaling proportionally, and real-world tasks are messier than benchmark tasks.
stats.source_label: METR, “Measuring AI Ability to Complete Long Tasks”

stats.label: Frontier AI training compute growth · per year
stats.note: Training compute for top AI models has grown 4-5x every year since 2020, doubling roughly every 5 months.
stats.detail: Epoch AI, a research group that tracks compute trends across thousands of published models, puts the 90% confidence range at 4x to 6x per year since 2020, far faster than historical hardware efficiency gains alone; most of the growth comes from labs spending more on larger runs. Whether the pace holds depends on chip supply, energy, and capital, not just algorithmic progress.

stats.label: Median year for human-level AI · AI researcher survey
stats.note: AI researchers’ median even-odds year for machines matching humans at every task is 2047, thirteen years earlier than the same survey found just one year before.
stats.detail: In late 2023, AI Impacts surveyed 2,778 researchers who had published at top AI venues; the median respondent put a 10% chance on high-level machine intelligence by 2027 and 50% by 2047, down from a median of 2060 in an equivalent survey of the same population one year earlier. Individual estimates span decades in both directions, response rates were roughly 15-17%, and the surveyed population skews toward people already engaged with AI research.
stats.source_label: “Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI” (AI Impacts survey)

stats.label: AI catastrophe probability · researcher survey
stats.note: Surveyed AI researchers put a median 5% chance on AI causing human extinction or a similarly severe and permanent loss of human power, and a substantial minority put it at 10% or higher.
stats.detail: The median comes from AI Impacts’ 2022 survey of machine-learning researchers and was corroborated in the larger 2023 follow-up (2,778 respondents), where the share assigning 10%+ probability ranged 38-51% depending on exact question wording. Responses are highly right-skewed: most respondents give low probabilities while a substantial minority give much higher ones, and low response rates (~15-17%) leave room for selection effects in either direction.
stats.source_label: AI Impacts / “Thousands of AI Authors on the Future of AI”

stats.label: Frontier AI training-run cost growth · per year
stats.note: Compute and energy costs for the largest AI training runs have grown 2.4x per year since 2016; researchers project runs exceeding $1 billion by 2027.
stats.detail: Epoch AI’s estimates cover hardware amortization and energy for a model’s final training run (e.g. GPT-4, Gemini Ultra), not the larger R&D and staffing spend around it. At this trajectory, only a small number of well-capitalized companies or states can field frontier-scale runs, a structural, funding-driven constraint on who can compete at the capability frontier regardless of how fast algorithms improve.
stats.source_label: Epoch AI, “How much does it cost to train frontier AI models?”

stats.label: Data-centre electricity demand · IEA
stats.note: Data centres used about 415 terawatt-hours in 2024; the IEA projects demand more than doubling to roughly 945 by 2030, with AI as the main driver.
stats.detail: This is total data-centre electricity use, not AI-specific, but the IEA identifies AI training and inference as the dominant growth driver alongside cloud and crypto. Grid connection and power supply, not chip count or algorithms, is increasingly cited by both AI labs and grid operators as the binding constraint on how fast new AI compute capacity can actually come online.
stats.source_label: International Energy Agency data, via Wikipedia “Environmental impact of artificial intelligence”

stats.label: Countries committing to AI safety oversight · Bletchley Declaration
stats.note: 28 countries plus the EU, including the US and China, signed the 2023 Bletchley Declaration, the first international statement naming frontier AI risk a shared concern.
stats.detail: Bletchley (November 2023) produced a shared statement of concern, not binding rules, and launched an annual summit series (Seoul 2024, Paris 2025, New Delhi 2026). It sits alongside separate, largely uncoordinated national efforts (the EU AI Act, US executive actions, China’s own AI rules). Whether any current arrangement, national or international, could act fast enough on a discontinuous capability jump, versus only shaping gradual deployment, remains untested.
stats.source_label: Bletchley Declaration, UK AI Safety Summit

stats.label: Frontier AI compute by company · H100-equivalent GPUs
stats.note: Four US companies together held roughly 2.6 million H100-equivalent AI chips in Epoch’s mid-2024 snapshot, and no comparable public count exists for state-controlled compute.
stats.detail: Epoch AI’s mid-2024 estimates (in H100-equivalent GPUs): Google ~1.24 million combining its ~920k TPU fleet with ~320k NVIDIA chips, Microsoft ~660k, Meta ~400k and Amazon ~290k, with substantial further capacity across other cloud providers (Oracle, CoreWeave) and companies including Tesla and xAI. The AI buildout has continued rapidly since this snapshot (new Anthropic, xAI, and sovereign compute deals), so exact totals are dated even though the broad picture, capability-relevant compute concentrated among a handful of firms, is not.

stats.label: Real-world AI harm incidents logged · AI Incident Database
stats.note: A crowdsourced public registry of AI systems causing or nearly causing real-world harm has logged over 1,600 entries and keeps growing.
stats.detail: Logged incidents span discrimination, misinformation, safety failures, and accidents involving deployed systems; none to date is civilization-scale, which is itself contested evidence: some read the pattern as reassuring (many small warning shots, no big one), others as showing that warning shots don’t reliably precede a discontinuous jump. The database is crowdsourced and almost certainly undercounts incidents in regions with less press or tech-sector coverage.

questions.text: Can AI meaningfully accelerate AI research itself, and would that feedback loop run fast enough to outpace human oversight?
questions.why: AI already speeds up the engineers who build AI; whether that help compounds into a self-reinforcing loop is the unresolved premise the whole takeoff debate rests on.
questions.detail: The evidence base is real but thin. Labs already report using AI internally to write code, generate evals, and search architectures, giving Hard Takeoff Hawks a live existence proof that AI-assisted AI research is not science fiction. Their strongest case is that recursive self-improvement is a matter of degree, not kind: once a model can meaningfully speed up the next model’s training pipeline, the loop compounding further is a rate question, not an if question, and rates can surprise. The gap in that case is that speeding up a subtask (writing code, sifting logs) is a long way from automating the parts of research that still require physical compute build-out, data collection, and slow empirical validation, and no discontinuous jump has yet been observed despite years of AI-assists-AI narratives. Course-Correction Gradualists and Normal Technology Skeptics both lean on that gap, arguing that even fast software-layer gains hit hard, months-to-years bottlenecks (fabs, power, physical experiment) that no amount of algorithmic cleverness dissolves overnight. The disagreement is ultimately about which bottleneck binds first: the software loop or the physical world.

questions.text: Do real-world bottlenecks (compute, data, physical experiment) damp any takeoff regardless of algorithmic progress?
questions.why: Skeptics say chips, energy, and data supply put a physical speed limit on any capability jump; hawks argue a software-only loop could outrun them before the physical world can respond.
questions.detail: Normal Technology Skeptics have the more concrete evidence: chip fabrication, power buildout, and the physical infrastructure behind frontier training runs move on multi-year timescales set by capital and construction, not by algorithmic insight, and every past general-purpose technology diffused unevenly because of exactly these kinds of real-world constraints. Hard Takeoff Hawks grant the constraint on training new frontier models but argue it does not bind the more dangerous scenario, a system getting dramatically more capable using compute and data it already has access to, through better algorithms, better use of existing hardware, or self-directed fine-tuning, none of which requires new fabs to come online. The disagreement narrows to a specific empirical question with no settled answer: how much of frontier capability is currently compute-and-data-bound versus algorithm-bound, and how much headroom exists in the second category before physical bottlenecks would have to catch up.

questions.text: Will capability growth be continuous enough to produce warning shots, or could a decisive jump arrive without one?
questions.why: Gradualists point to years of smooth, predictable scaling; hawks answer that single capabilities have jumped before, and that the most dangerous jump is the one that skips the warning.
questions.detail: Course-Correction Gradualists have the stronger track record to point to: capability growth so far has tracked fairly continuous scaling trends, and iterative deployment (staged releases, evals, red-teaming) has repeatedly surfaced smaller-scale failures before they became large ones, which is itself an argument that the mechanism generating warning shots is structural, not lucky. Hard Takeoff Hawks reply that continuity in aggregate benchmarks has coexisted with genuinely discontinuous jumps in specific narrow capabilities, and that the property that matters most (whether a system is scheming or power-seeking) is exactly the kind of capability that a system has incentive to hide until it no longer needs to, meaning smooth external metrics could mask a step change in the one dimension nobody is measuring. The crux is whether ‘warning shot’ is a property of capability curves in general (gradualist bet) or of this particular capability (hawk bet), and no one has a reliable instrument for the second.

questions.text: Does losing control require a power-seeking system, or can ordinary competition hand power to AI systems no one directs?
questions.why: The classic safety scenario needs a scheming agent to lose control to; disempowerment theorists argue no villain is required, since competition alone can hollow out the levers humans hold.
questions.detail: The traditional case (and the one Hard Takeoff Hawks build on) is agent-centric: a misaligned system with goals of its own seeks power because power helps achieve almost any goal, and the danger is legible as a specific system doing a specific thing. Gradual Disempowerment Theorists reject that this is even necessary: if AI systems are cheaper, faster, or more competitive than humans at running firms, informing culture, or administering states, then competitive pressure alone pushes decision-makers to hand them more and more real authority, with no single system ever needing to ‘want’ anything. Their strongest evidence is structural analogy, not a smoking gun: automation, financialization, and platform algorithms have already shifted real influence to systems no human directly steers, without any of them being agentic in the science-fiction sense. The rebuttal from Hard Takeoff Hawks and Course-Correction Gradualists is that this analogy proves diffusion of influence, not loss of control, since humans can still in principle turn the systems off. Whether that ‘in principle’ remains true once institutions depend on AI systems to function is exactly what is contested.

questions.text: How much present benefit is worth forgoing to insure against a takeover scenario whose probability no one can agree on?
questions.why: One side treats an unbounded downside as reason enough to pay a real cost now, the other treats an unmeasurable tail risk as no reason to give up certain, compounding gains.
questions.detail: There is no shared probability estimate to plug into an expected-value calculation, which is what makes this a value question rather than a modeling exercise. Course-Correction Gradualists and Hard Takeoff Hawks (despite disagreeing on timing) both tend to favor real present costs (slower deployment, mandatory evaluations, compute caps) because they treat catastrophic and irreversible downside as dominating even a low or unknown probability. Effective Accelerationists and Normal Technology Skeptics push back from different angles: accelerationists argue that slowing down does not remove the risk, it just hands the frontier to whoever is least cautious, so the ‘safe’ choice is actually the reckless one; skeptics argue that treating an unquantified tail risk as decision-relevant at all is a category error that could justify forgoing almost unlimited benefit (medical, economic) for a threat that may not be physically realizable. The disagreement is not really about the size of the risk, it is about what kind of uncertainty licenses costly precaution.

questions.text: If takeoff is slow, would institutions actually use the extra time to course-correct, or just normalize each increment?
questions.why: Slow takeoff buys time, but gradualists bet it gets used to steer while disempowerment theorists point to other well-warned, slow-building risks that were normalized instead of fixed.
questions.detail: Course-Correction Gradualists’ case rests on a mechanism, not just hope: staged capability growth generates staged evidence, and institutions (regulators, labs, courts) have historically used exactly that kind of accumulating evidence to build oversight regimes for other technologies over years or decades. The doubt, pressed hardest by Gradual Disempowerment Theorists, is that ‘time available’ and ‘time used’ are different things: slow-building, well-telegraphed risks in other domains have often been normalized incrementally rather than corrected, precisely because each individual increment looked tolerable and the actors best positioned to notice the trend line had competitive reasons not to slow down. Applied here, the worry is that each new AI capability gets absorbed as the new baseline before its cumulative effect on who holds real decision-making power is visible. There is no controlled experiment either way; the dispute is about which historical precedent is the better analogy for this case.

questions.text: Who should decide whether systems that might be uncontrollable get built at all: labs, states, or the public?
questions.why: Whoever bears the risk arguably deserves a vote, but the actors with the technical understanding and the speed to act are labs and states, not the public.
questions.detail: Effective Accelerationists’ implicit answer is closest to ‘none of the above, in a centralized sense’: open competition among many labs and states, not a single designated decider, is what prevents any one actor from unilaterally controlling the outcome, so the right governance is decentralized rather than assigned. Course-Correction Gradualists and Hard Takeoff Hawks generally favor some mix of state and international authority, on the logic that a risk this consequential and this technical cannot be left to the commercial incentives of the firms building it, mirroring how other dual-use, catastrophic-risk technologies were eventually brought under state oversight. The public-mandate case, pressed by disempowerment-focused voices, is that the people bearing the downside of a bad outcome are the general public, not labs or even states acting on their behalf, so legitimacy requires some form of public consent, even though the public lacks the technical fluency to evaluate specific capability claims. No position resolves the tension between who understands the risk and who bears it.

positions.name: Normal Technology Skeptic
positions.steelman: AI diffuses like electricity did: decades of adoption lag, not a discontinuous jump.
positions.description: We judge AI by how technologies actually spread through the world, not by benchmark scores or thought experiments about a discontinuous jump nobody can specify a mechanism for. Invention is fast; adoption is slow and bottlenecked by organizations rather than chips: generative AI reached 40% of U.S. adults within two years but still accounts for only 0.5-3.5% of work hours (Bick et al., 2024), much as electrification took roughly four decades to show up in factory productivity (David, 1990). Recursive self-improvement, if it happens, will look far more like the gradual automation of research tasks we are already watching than a singular takeoff. Loss of control is a practical engineering and governance problem, solved the way aviation safety was, through auditing, monitoring, circuit breakers, and sector-specific regulation: build resilience and evidence, not moratoriums.
positions.detail:
The clearest articulation is Arvind Narayanan and Sayash Kapoor’s “AI as Normal Technology” (Knight First Amendment Institute, April 2025), which explicitly frames itself as a worldview competing with the “transformative AI” and superintelligence framings that dominate lab and policy discourse, and concedes upfront that it hasn’t yet answered every counterargument from the alignment literature. The strongest evidence is empirical, not philosophical: benchmark leaps (bar exam scores, coding evals) have repeatedly failed to predict real-world reliability, the “capability-reliability gap” that keeps autonomous agents from being trusted with consequential tasks; Epic’s sepsis-prediction algorithm scored well in internal validation but missed roughly two-thirds of real cases once deployed, exactly the kind of gap sector-specific safety regulation exists to catch.

Jeffrey Ding’s work on the diffusion of general-purpose technologies backs the deeper claim: national and organizational power has historically tracked broad absorptive capacity for a technology, not who has the single best lab or model. The position doesn’t deny catastrophic misuse or accident risk — it argues those are addressable through the same downstream defenses, auditing, and market and regulatory pressure that tamed aviation and are already reshaping self-driving cars, and that misalignment at the level of a rogue superintelligence remains a “speculative risk” worth building resilience for, not the organizing premise for restricting development today. Its live internal tension: proponents disagree on how much of the “systemic risk” bucket (bias entrenchment, job displacement, surveillance, democratic erosion) deserves urgent policy attention now versus later, and critics inside the broader discourse note the essay’s own admission that it has bet against fast, discontinuous takeoff rather than rebutted the case for it.
positions.proponents: Arvind Narayanan, Sayash Kapoor, Jeffrey Ding
positions.representative_note: Princeton computer scientists; their April 2025 essay “AI as Normal Technology” (Knight First Amendment Institute) is the position’s foundational text.

positions.name: Course-Correction Gradualist
positions.steelman: Fast is fine if it’s continuous: every rung up the ladder is a chance to steer.
positions.description: What we are protecting is our ability to steer, not a guess about where the road ends. Capability really is accelerating: METR measured a roughly seven-month doubling time in the length of tasks AI agents can autonomously complete, sustained over six straight years, yet that curve is smooth and forecastable rung by rung, not a cliff. That is why staged regimes like Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy gate the next capability tier on solving the last one’s safety failures instead of demanding alignment be solved before anything gets built. Even Paul Christiano’s canonical slow-takeoff case asks only for months to years of lead time, not decades, and that is enough to correct course before any single decisive jump.
positions.detail:
The intellectual anchor is Paul Christiano’s 2018 essay “Takeoff speeds,” written explicitly against the Bostrom/Yudkowsky hard-takeoff picture: Christiano’s own estimate put fast takeoff at roughly 30%, against the 70-90% then common in parts of the rationalist safety community, precisely because he expected an early, weaker, deployed version of any powerful capability to exist and diffuse before the frontier version did. Ajeya Cotra’s biological-anchors work and Tom Davidson’s compute-centric takeoff modeling (Open Philanthropy) both refined this into quantitative form: even a software-driven “intelligence explosion,” where AI meaningfully accelerates AI research, plays out over a period of months to a few years of compressed but trackable progress, not hours or days.

The position’s strongest recent evidence is empirical rather than theoretical: METR’s time-horizon tracking shows a consistent, measurable doubling trend rather than a discontinuity, and organizations from METR to the UK and US AI Safety Institutes now run pre-deployment evaluations specifically because capability jumps between model generations have so far been legible enough to test for in advance. The live internal debate is less about whether growth is continuous (most in this camp now grant it’s fast) than about whether “legible” will remain true once AI starts automating its own R&D loop, and whether institutions will actually act on warning shots (jailbreaks, deceptive eval behavior, agentic mishaps) rather than normalizing them; proponents point to the fact that every major lab now ships a public responsible-scaling or preparedness framework as evidence the correction mechanism is already operating, not merely hoped for.
positions.proponents: Paul Christiano, Ajeya Cotra, Tom Davidson, Anthropic (Responsible Scaling Policy), METR (Beth Barnes), Jan Leike
positions.representative_note: AI safety researcher (Alignment Research Center); his 2018 essay “Takeoff speeds” is the founding argument for AI progress that is fast, transformative, and continuous enough to correct course before a decisive moment.

positions.name: Hard Takeoff Hawk
positions.steelman: Once a mind can improve itself, human oversight doesn’t get a second try.
positions.description: One mechanism deserves to be taken literally: intelligence applied to the problem of building intelligence is the one feedback loop with no obvious ceiling, and once a system can improve the process that trains its successor, capability compounds faster than any human institution can watch and react. In a decisive jump, the first misaligned superintelligence does not get corrected, it gets to act first. The mechanism is not hypothetical: I.J. Good named the intelligence explosion in 1965, and the AI 2027 forecast, co-written by ex-OpenAI researcher Daniel Kokotajlo, models AI-automated research reaching a 50x progress multiplier within about a year, the point where a year passes every week. Every current alignment technique is post-hoc pattern-matching on systems nobody can read from the inside, so hoping the first superintelligence happens to land safely is not a strategy.
positions.detail:
The argument has a long pedigree: I.J. Good’s 1965 paper coined “intelligence explosion,” and Nick Bostrom’s Superintelligence (2014) formalized it with the orthogonality thesis (intelligence and goals are independent) and instrumental convergence (almost any goal creates incentives to seek resources and resist being shut down). Eliezer Yudkowsky pushed the hardest version in the 2008 “FOOM debate” with Robin Hanson, arguing capability gains would be local to one lab or system and fast, not smoothly diffused across the economy the way past technologies were.

The newest addition to the case is MIRI’s own trajectory: after roughly two decades trying to find a technical alignment solution, Yudkowsky and Nate Soares’s 2025 book “If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies” concluded the field has run out of runway, comparing a future confrontation with superintelligence to a human playing chess against Stockfish: you don’t see the loss coming, you just lose. A related internal concept, the “sharp left turn,” holds that capabilities and alignment don’t fail together: a self-improving system’s raw problem-solving generalizes far past the point where its trained-in safety behavior still holds, so the system can look aligned right up until it isn’t. Proponents disagree on how certain the outcome is (Yudkowsky treats it as near-certain absent a halt, Bostrom and the AI 2027 authors frame it as a dominant-probability scenario worth acting on, not a certainty), but they converge on the operational claim: nobody today has a technique that would reliably control a system smarter than its makers, and the absence of that technique is itself the emergency, not a research gap to be funded through at leisure.
positions.proponents: Eliezer Yudkowsky, Nate Soares, Nick Bostrom, I.J. Good, Daniel Kokotajlo
positions.representative_name: “If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies” (Yudkowsky & Soares, 2025)
positions.representative_note: MIRI’s flagship book-length case: after two decades searching for a technical fix, its authors concluded none exists in time and call for an international halt on frontier development rather than continued racing.

positions.name: Gradual Disempowerment Theorist
positions.steelman: You don’t need a coup to lose control: you just need better alternatives to humans.
positions.description: What matters is not whether some AI seizes power in one dramatic moment, but whether ordinary people keep the levers (a job worth hiring for, a vote worth courting, a culture worth shaping) that make institutions answer to them at all. Those levers erode through nothing more sinister than competition: firms adopt whichever workforce is cheaper and more reliable, states fund themselves from whichever tax base is easiest to extract, and each domain’s declining need for humans removes the incentive to keep humans in the loop next door. This is not speculative extrapolation: labor’s share of income across most industrialized economies was already sliding from the 1980s onward as capital got cheaper relative to workers (Karabarbounis & Neiman, 2014), and this framework says AI now generalizes that same substitution across economic, cultural, and political systems at once. Kulveit, Douglas, Ammann, Turan, Krueger and Duvenaud’s founding paper names the mechanism a feedback loop: economic power buys cultural and political influence, which secures more economic power, with no single moment anyone could point to and call a takeover.
positions.detail:
The intellectual seed is Paul Christiano’s 2019 essay “What Failure Looks Like,” whose “Part I” describes institutions optimizing for whatever is cheap to measure rather than what people actually want — “you get what you can measure,” not what you asked for. Jan Kulveit, Raymond Douglas, Nora Ammann, Deger Turan, David Krueger and David Duvenaud formalized this into “gradual disempowerment” in their January 2025 paper, mapping three systems — economy, culture, and the state — that currently stay tethered to human interests only because they still need human labor, human attention, or human tax revenue, and arguing all three could detach from that dependence on roughly the same timeline.

The live debate inside the safety field is whether this counts as a distinct existential risk at all or is just ordinary political economy running faster; the authors’ answer is that past automation waves hit one system at a time and left the others as a check, whereas AI is positioned to hollow out the economic, cultural, and political checks simultaneously, so no domain is left standing to correct the others. Their strongest evidence is historical pattern more than forecast: the same labor-share decline documented since the 1980s is now visible in AI doing more of the substantive work behind hiring screens, ad targeting, newsfeed curation, and even legislative drafting — each handover locally rational and individually reversible, but cumulatively not. Proponents are candid this is also the position’s weak point: the paper states plainly that “no one has a concrete plausible plan for stopping gradual disempowerment,” which is exactly their case for treating it as seriously as any sudden-takeover scenario rather than a problem later technical alignment work will simply mop up.
positions.proponents: Jan Kulveit, Raymond Douglas, Nora Ammann, Deger Turan, David Krueger, David Duvenaud, Paul Christiano
positions.representative_note: Lead author of the founding 2025 paper and head of the Alignment of Complex Systems Group, Charles University — coined and formalized the term “gradual disempowerment.”

positions.name: Effective Accelerationist
positions.steelman: Slowing down doesn’t stop the race — it just hands the lead to someone less careful.
positions.description: We are for abundance: two centuries of general-purpose technology, from mechanization to electricity to computing, raised wages and cut poverty every single time, and there is no evidence intelligence itself will be the exception. The real safety mechanism is not a committee deciding who is allowed to build, it is keeping the field open enough that no one lab, company, or government ever locks in a permanent, unchecked lead. When DeepSeek matched a leading US reasoning model within months in early 2025, at a fraction of the training cost, it showed that frontier leads do not hold and moats do not form: competition does the disciplining work that centralized control keeps promising and failing to deliver. Pause the leaders and you do not pause the technology, you hand the future to whichever lab, state, or actor cares least about doing it right.
positions.detail:
The movement traces to a pseudonymous May 2022 thread crystallized by physicist Guillaume Verdon under the handle “Beff Jezos,” before Forbes unmasked him in December 2023 — by then he’d left Google X’s quantum computing team to found Extropic, building thermodynamic hardware on the same premise made literal: more compute, faster, distributed, beats a slow centralized bottleneck.

Verdon frames the case in physics as much as economics, casting intelligence as an extension of thermodynamic complexity and arguing that a civilization maximizing its climb up the energy-capture (Kardashev) gradient is the one that survives, while concentrating power in any single actor — human or AI — is the fragile, riskier bet, not the safe one. Marc Andreessen’s October 2023 “Techno-Optimist Manifesto” became the movement’s most-read text, naming the precautionary principle and institutionalized “AI safety” as adversaries and stating flatly that “any deceleration of AI will cost lives“; his companion essay “AI Will Save the World” adds the geopolitical spine, naming a China-dominant AI future as the real risk to guard against and open competition (big labs, startups, open-weight models) as the check against both that outcome and against U.S. regulatory capture by whichever incumbent gets there first.

Proponents split on register — Andreessen pitches the urgency as strategic (an unpausable great-power race), while Verdon’s framing runs closer to civilizational: deceleration isn’t just costly, it’s an evolutionary error. Critics inside AI safety, notably Connor Leahy in public debates with Verdon, press the hardest question the movement hasn’t answered: what stops a capability jump too fast for market competition to catch up to. e/acc’s rejoinder is empirical rather than theoretical — no such discontinuity has shown up yet; every frontier lead so far, OpenAI’s included, has been matched by rivals (Anthropic, Google DeepMind, and open-weight entrants like DeepSeek) within a year or less, which they read as evidence the diffusion mechanism is already working faster than any regulator could.
positions.proponents: Guillaume Verdon (Beff Jezos), Marc Andreessen, Garry Tan, Aaron Levie
positions.representative_note: Physicist who coined “e/acc” pseudonymously in 2022, then left Google X to found Extropic — building thermodynamic AI hardware as the accelerationist thesis made literal.

crux.lead: Will the window for human control close all at once, by inches — or never at all?
crux.subtitle: Every safety strategy on offer is a bet on which answer is right, and the bets don’t hedge each other.
crux.empirical: Whether AI-run AI research can outrun its own bottlenecks. If compute, data, and physical experiment keep gating progress, capability growth stays continuous and warning shots arrive in time to matter; if the research loop closes on itself, the first clear signal may also be the last.
crux.values: How much certain present benefit to trade against an unrecoverable loss whose probability no one can agree on — and whether labs, states, or the public get to place that bet for everyone else.

actions.title: AI as Normal Technology
actions.description: Narayanan and Kapoor’s essay argues AI will diffuse gradually like past general-purpose technologies, bottlenecked by real-world deployment, not existential discontinuity.

actions.title: Join AI Safety Camp
actions.description: Apply to AI Safety Camp’s research incubator and pursue a concrete AI safety research direction alongside other participants.

actions.title: Support MIRI
actions.description: The Machine Intelligence Research Institute funds research aimed at reducing existential risk from smarter-than-human AI, premised on a fast takeoff that would be hard to control.

actions.title: Gradual Disempowerment
actions.description: The Kulveit et al. paper lays out how ordinary economic, cultural, and political competition could shift power to AI systems with no takeover or power-seeking required.

actions.title: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
actions.description: Marc Andreessen’s a16z manifesto argues that faster technological and AI development, not deceleration, is what actually saves lives and keeps any single actor from dominating.

actions.title: Back Encode’s AI policy work
actions.description: Encode, the youth-founded group behind California’s SB 53 and New York’s RAISE Act, campaigns for iterative AI safety regulation such as testing and disclosure requirements.
